CAMPING BOOKS 


LIGHT FROM A 

THOUSAND CAMPFIRES 

The problem of expanding popula¬ 
tion and its possible effects on 
camping 

The place of religion in camping 
How camps can be used the year- 
round 

What goes into a well-balanced 
camp program 

What counselors feel are the most 
important factors in maintaining 
a contented staff 

Camp as a return to nature for chil¬ 
dren brought up in urban culture 
How to realize a camper's potential 
through your program 
The rewards from working with handi¬ 
capped children 

How to sustain the positive effects 
of camping throughout the year 

And more . . . 

For this and many reasons, you’ll want to own 
LIGHT FROM A THOUSAND CAMPFIRES. In its 
glow, you will find light shed upon a whole new 
world—a world of comradeship, joy, strength, 
romance, laughter, beauty and understanding. 
Camping is the cultivation of the richest potential 
of the human spirit. For anyone whose lively 
curiosity sparks an interest in all that concerns 
children, this book will have a deep and lasting 
significance. 



"CAMPING IS 

EDUCATION" 

We have no question but that this 
will prove to be a classic of camping 
literature. Many letters of praise have 
been received, one of which states 
that "the message contained is of such 
an important nature that it should be 
mailed to every person in the country 
connected with education." 

75 * 


THE UNIQUE MISSION 
OF THE SUMMER CAMP 

In the words of Fred Rogers, ACA 
President: "Would that every camp 
related person might read this beauti¬ 
ful treatise on camping. In these 
days of materialism, urbanization, 
mechanization, conformity, and super¬ 
ficial living, it is good to have the 
Dean of Camping, C. Walton Johnson, 
bring into clear focus the real purpose, 
philosophy, and mission of the sum¬ 
mer camp."

WINTER CAMPING 
FOR CANADIAN YOUTH 

W . E. Yard, 

Director, Camp Pinecrest . 


Whenever camp people meet to 
discuss camping objectives we find 
them reviewing the remarkable oppor¬ 
tunities which camp life presents for 
helping youngsters to acquire specific 
skills; helping them to get along with 
one another; helping them to accept 
the responsibilities that go with living 
in a camp community; helping them to 
gain a greater appreciation for the 
spiritual values; and then . . . over and 
over again ... we hear camp people 
stating their objective to teach young¬ 
sters to live more comfortably in the 
out of doors. 

“To live more comfortably in the 
out of doors” .... Sometimes we 
feel this should be stated “to live more 
comfortably in the out of doors when 
the out of doors is comfortable.” July 
and August certainly are those two 
months in the year when one can most 
comfortably live under canvas, on the 
trail, or at the canoe trip camp site. 
Most of our present-day children’s 
camps provide good cabin sleeping 
accommodation and covered recreation 
areas ... a practice which is certainly 
well justified since our children come 
from city homes. The process of teach¬ 
ing them to live, play and be thor¬ 
oughly comfortable out of doors is a 
gradual one, and it is not likely to be 
accomplished happily by throwing them 
out into a “rugged environment”. The 
unfortunate fact about many of our 
camps is that we operate only during 
July and August when, as indicated, 


living in the out of doors comfortably 
is probably quite easy. 

Recognising that for most children’s 
camps it is not economical to open and 
close each weekend through Spring and 
Fall, and also that most facilities are 
impractical for use during the colder 
seasons of the year, it is still interesting 
to observe that more and more camps 
are making use of their facilities for 
recreational purposes on weekends 
other than in July and August. In a 
recent survey of thirty three Y.M.G.A. 
camps in Canada it was indicated that 
twenty seven open for weekend groups 
on occasion. 

In another article in this issue of 
Canadian Camping one of our directors 
points out some ways in which build¬ 
ings can be winterized at a very limited 
cost. Catering to small weekend or 
Christmas holiday groups requires, of 
course, certain facilities which are not 
essential during the warm summer 
months. These facilities can be pro¬ 
vided without extravagant outlays, but 
it is unlikely that camp directors will 
make these adjustments in their faci¬ 
lities unless they are convinced of the 
values in taking groups to camp in the 
months from September through to 
June. It is doubtful whether the mone¬ 
tary returns from winter and weekend 
camping justify the time and effort 
that would be involved in embarking 
on this program. However there is un¬ 
deniable evidence of the tremendous 


8 


Canadian Camping 



values that can accrue to younsters, to 
camp staffs and in fact to the whole 
camp organization through these winter 
and weekend camp programs. 

In Fall and Spring there are many 
lessons to be learned from nature. 
Nothing is static in the out of doors 
at this time. The glorious colours of 
the Fall and the busy scurrying about 
of every creature in preparation for 
the Winter, provide lessons galore for 
children. Similarly the great awaken¬ 
ing of the Spring with the myriads of 
buds, wild flowers, and the return of 
the birds, present further lessons which 
can form the beginning of life-long 
interests. Perhaps Winter itself pro¬ 
vides the opportunity for the greatest 
satisfactions to youngsters in learning 
to live comfortably in the out of doors. 
Surely no one would suggest that we 
take city youngsters and have them 
“rough it” in rustic shelters under 
extreme winter conditions. On the con 
trary, it is important that the “home 
base” be thoroughly comfortable and 
that the leadership has the kind of 
skills and insights which will help the 
youngsters little by little acquire the 
ability to take care of themselves, in 
fact to enjoy themselves under these 
extreme conditions. 

The skills of snow-shoeing and of 
cross country skiing are of course syn¬ 
onymous with winter camping. Certain 
areas such as marshes and bogs which 
a camper would never travel in the 
summer time are now easily traversed. 
The sport of orienteering, with map 
and compass, takes on new dimensions, 
as youngsters can draw a direct line on 
a distant object and travel there over 
hills and hazards. The tracks of birds 
and wild life are there for all to see 
during the winter months and many a 
story can be read from the markings 
along every trail. 

New interests develop in the industry 
of the Northland . . . How is ice cut 


and stored? What happens to the 
tree from the time it is cut until it finds 
its way into our home as a plank or 
board? How can a trapper possibly 
make a living when one so seldom sees 
a Beaver or a Muskrat or Otter? What 
happens to those animals, fishes and 
reptiles that disappeared throughout 
these cold winter months? Will it snow 
to-morrow? How can we forecast the 
change in the weather? What kind of 
wood makes the best and quickest fire 
in the winter time? All these and 
many, many other questions provide 
the basis for the educational aspects 
of a program which, if we really be¬ 
lieve that we should be teaching 
youngsters to live comfortably in the 
out of doors, becomes somewhat of an 
obligation for each one of us in the 
camping field. 

Winter camping is almost certain to 
be short-term camping and yet in 
experiences in this field both in British 
Columbia and in Ontario we have 
found that staff have a unique oppor¬ 
tunity to affect youngsters in the winter 
camp setting. It seems that the self- 
evident need to acquire the “primitive 
skills” provides an unusually powerful 
incentive for learning, This is certainly 
a program with the challenge, ancl 
adventure to catch the interest of the 
older boy or girl ... an interest that 
has frequently faltered where conven¬ 
tional summer camping programs are 
concerned. 

Some of our youth-serving agencies 
have been doing winter camping of one 
kind and another for many years. How 
ever the camping movement has yet to 
recognise the full potential both for 
leaders and for campers in the attrac¬ 
tive, adventuresome winter camping 
field. Why not attempt a “pilot pro¬ 
ject” in your camp this winter. Your 
campers will be the leaders for the 
winter camping programs of the future! 


Toronto , Canada , December , 1960 


9 


THE VALUE 
OF CAMPING 
FOR THE 
CRIPPLED 
CHILD 

Tony Shorgan, Camp Director, 

The Province of Quebec Society 
For Crippled Children, Inc., 

Crippled Children’s Camp at 

St. Alphonse de Joliette, Que., Canada. 


What is a crippled child ? A crippled 
child is a child who, although handi¬ 
capped physically, has the same needs 
as any other child, which are to have 
friends and affection, fun, laughter, 
and to enjoy life. The weakness in his 
physical constitution does not mean he 
is necessarily limited in his intelligence, 
spiritual and emotional capacity, or 
ambition. However, it is essential that 
he be provided with the facilities vital 
for the development of these qualities, 
and this is one of the primary objec¬ 
tives of a Crippled Children’s Camp. 


Many people are inclined to over¬ 
protect a crippled child. This should 
be avoided, as it prevents him from 
becoming self-reliant. Why fear that 
by letting a crippled child do things 
for himself he will be harmed physic¬ 
ally? Is it not natural for any child to 
get hurt once in a while — at play, at 
school, or in the home? For the crip¬ 
pled child, as for any child, it is often 
much less serious to get hurt physically 
than to be hurt emotionally by over¬ 
protection. 

Unfortunately a crippled child living 
in a city neighbourhood, where he is 
surrounded by children who are 
stronger physically, is apt to be very 
isolated. The physically strong child 
does not understand the crippled child 
and cannot realize what it is not to be 
able to run as fast as others, or to be 
totally unable to walk. Therefore, when 
team or group games are organized in 
the community, the crippled child is 
left out because he cannot run as fast, 
or throw a ball as far, as other children 
can In any sports (amateur or pro¬ 
fessional) the superior performer is 
popular with everyone but a poor per¬ 
former is forgotten, ignored, and per¬ 
haps eventually not included in the 
team. When a crippled child is cut off 
from the activities of other children 
around him he lives in a dark and 
solitary world. His friends are not 
nearly so plentiful as those of a physic¬ 
ally well child, because it is so much 
harder for him to make friends. 

These less fortunate children must 
have the opportunity to strengthen 
their initiative and characters normally. 
By having access to the proper means 
(provided in large measure by camp 
life) a crippled child will develop as 
well as other children and may even 
surpass them by way of compensation 
for his handicap. It is also much more 
important that this type of child have 
the opportunity for his mental and 
emotional evolution than for any other 


10 


Canadian Camping 



child because, in many cases, he has 
spent months or years in hospitals 
where the activities are very limited. 
Due to the previous restricted life he 
has led, camping is indispensable for 
the growth of the crippled child. It 
opens up new horizons and is the road 
to a new life where he is given the 
chance to do many things which, to 
him, formerly seemed to be impossible. 
For instance, all boys love to play ball. 
Before a crippled child comes to camp 
he may never have had a baseball bat 
in his hands, as the other children 
would not allow him on their team. 
It is, therefore, a real thrill for him to 
be able to take part in a ball game. 
At camp the physically handicapped 
child has many other little handi¬ 
capped friends, the staff, and, possibly, 
other children, around him laughing, 
singing, playing, arguing or disagreeing 
with him in a normal way. This com¬ 
radeship teaches him to give as well as 
receive. 

It is preferable for a physically 
handicapped child going to camp for 
the first time to attend a Crippled 
Children’s Camp, and not a camp for 
normal children, because in a camp for 
crippled children they have trained 
personnel who understand these child¬ 
ren and are able to prepare them to 
join in groups with other children, 
teach them to do things for them¬ 
selves, and to take part in various 
games and activities. A crippled child 
who has never had any previous camp¬ 
ing experience and who goes to a camp 
for normal children for the first time 
could have a very traumatic experi¬ 
ence, because there is a danger he will 
not be understood by the personnel or 
the other children. He would be more 
of a spectator than a participant. It is 
not normal for any child (crippled or 
otherwise) to live as a spectator. He 
must live as a participant. There is 
nothing more depressing for a child 
than to sit and watch others performing. 

Our Crippled Children’s Camp is the 


largest camp of its kind in North Amer¬ 
ica. At our camp, during the month of 
July, we have 280 boys from the age 
of two years to twenty-one years, 
suffering from all types of physical 
disabilities and, in the month of Aug¬ 
ust, a somewhat fewer number of girls. 
Some are able to walk, and even run, 
while other are confined to their beds. 
These children are lodged in thirty 
small huts, with an average of ten 
children to each hut. Many authorities 
in camping disagree with a camp hav¬ 
ing too large a number of children. I 
feel, however, there are advantages to 
a large camp. In a large camp we 
are able to organize teams to compete 
against one another, which is impos¬ 
sible in a small camp. If the children 
can run, we have games where they 
have the opportunity to do so; if con¬ 
fined to bed, we have bedside games, 
etc. In the large camp children have 
a chance to compare themselves with 
one another and often realize that some 
children with much more severe handi¬ 
caps can do better than they, which is 
an incentive to them to try harder. Of 
course, it is impossible for one program 
director to handle this whole task by 
himself. We delegate one person to be 
responsible for each group of children, 
which must not exceed some sixty in 
number. We have a ratio of 1 counsellor 
for every two or three campers. Having 
the camp divided into small groups 
permits of more individual attention. 
Our camping program is well deve¬ 
loped. Most of our campers follow the 
same schedule and activities as they 
would in a camp for normal children; 
such as, group games, campfires, swim¬ 
ming, boating, pony rides, archery, 
rifle shooting, overnight hikes (an 
activity enjoyed by all campers of ten 
years old and over despite the serious¬ 
ness of their disability), sing-songs, 
dramatics, movies, musical concerts, 
arts and crafts (pottery, weaving, 
woodcarving, sewing, embroidery, 

turn to page 38 


Toronto , Canada, December , 1960

MONEY IN THE BANK 

BUDGET, OR ELSE .... 

C. Labbett, 

■ . - ■ Director, Camp Oconto. 


The Captain of a ship must chart his 
course across the sea in order to reach 
his destination and in the same manner 
a camp director must chart his financial 
course to guide him through the year. 
Storms, other ships, fog and other 
emergencies may cause the captain to 
deviate from his original course and 
destination but as soon as possible he 
will return to his original course. The 
program director of a camp has a 
broad plan in his mind of what he 
wishes to accomplish during the sum¬ 
mer and while he may deviate from it 
at various times he still comes back to 
his original plan and continues to his 
goal. Without a financial path to fol¬ 
low and a goal to reach, the financial 
aspect of camping is like a ship with¬ 
out a course or destination to reach. 

This article is planned to give you 
some idea of how a budget can be set 
up and used as a tool in reaching the 
financial goal. It will not cover this 
very large subject entirely by any 
means, and the remarks made will be 
in a general sense so that you will have 
to make allowances or adjustments for 
your particular camp or the province 
in which you operate. 

For camps that have been in oper¬ 
ation a few years and have kept a 
proper set of books, the drawing up of 
a budget is a simple matter. If you 
do not have books of account to keep. 


a proper written record of receipts 
and expenses, you would be wise to 
hire an accountant to advise you in 
this respect, — it will be money well 
spent. The accountant can, if you 
wish, check your books once a year, 
help you with income tax and also 
answer any questions you may have 
from time to time. The Department 
of National Revenue requires that you 
keep a written record of your business 
transactions in such a manner that they 
can be examined and understood by a 
government auditor at any time of the 
year. The Unemployment Insurance 
Commission and the Ontario Work¬ 
men’s Compensation Board also main¬ 
tain auditors who may examine your 
salary and wage records at any time. 

The first item to consider for a 
budget is Income or Receipts. The 
number of campers multiplied by the 
fee they will be paying, plus any tuck 
revenue, grants or other moneys re¬ 
ceived will make up this side of the 
Budget. Be conservative here -— it is 
better to err on the short side than be 
too optimistic and then not have the 
enrollment you hoped for. 

The Expenditure side can be classi¬ 
fied under the following headings •— 
give or take a few depending upon 
your particular camp and its operation. 
These headings may vary from year to 


12 


Canadian Camping 



year as your experience grows and con¬ 
ditions change. Also, the more detail 
you can have the better to pinpoint 
any item getting out of line. 

I would suggest you list them one 
under another with the amount of 
money off to the right of each item. 
The words in brackets are by way of 
explanation. 

Food 

Salaries and Wages (can be broken 
down into counsellors, kitchen, 
maintenance) 

Supplies (can also be broken into de¬ 
partments but will cover such 
items as soap, toilet paper, infirm¬ 
ary supplies, nails, brooms, ad 
infinitum). 

Insurance (fire, auto, burglary, busi¬ 
ness interruption, etc.) 

Repairs and Maintenance 
Telephone & Telegraph 
Fees and Donations 
Printing 
Office Supplies 
Office Rent 

Red Cross and Royal Life Saving So¬ 
ciety Examination Fees 

Travelling Expenses 

Publicity and Advertising 

Light, Heat and Power 

Tuck Purchases 

Vehicle Expenses 

Boat Expenses 

Freight and cartage 

Taxes, Mortgage or Loan Interest 

Bank Charges 


Unemployment Insurance and Work¬ 
men’s Compensation, (where ap¬ 
plicable) 

General Expense (for any items not 
classified above) 

Food and Wages will be the biggest 
expense items. The cost of your raw 
food can be anywhere from 75^ to 
$1.50 per day, depending upon many 
factors. Wages for counsellors, kit¬ 
chen and dining room staff and main¬ 
tenance will have to be thoroughly 
gone into and some type of wage scale 
is desirable. Go over last year’s staff 
and see whom you want back, and if 
they will come back, will their salary 
go up or be the same? Then decide 
how many more staff people will be 
required and how much they will have 
to be paid. The other expenses will be 
easily allocated to their proper column 
—do not try and fool yourself by placing 
them in the wrong column such as put¬ 
ting a miscellaneous food purchase 
under “miscellaneous expense” instead 
of “food”. The same headings that ap¬ 
pear in your budget should appear in 
your books so that transposition and 
comparison are easy. Add and balance 
the books weekly or monthly or when¬ 
ever you feel it is necessary to keep you 
well informed of the financial condition 
of your camp. Budgets are not meant 
to be absolute ceilings, or floors for 
that matter, on revenues and expenses 
but are to be used as a guide to allo¬ 
cate the correct amount of money to 
its proper place. If you are on a very 
strict or tight budget and you cannot 
help going over in some department 
due to an emergency, then measures 
should be taken to make up this 
amount from some other department 
or else get more revenue. After the 

turn to page 36 


Toronto , Canada , December , 1960

WHOQUZIT? 


WHO 

EVALUATES? 

W. E. Yard, 

Director s Camp Pinecrest. 


There is certainly no camp where 
evaluation of some sort does not take 
place. Evaluation may even be forced 
upon the Director by such circum¬ 
stances as insufficient financial return, 
low registrations, staff problems . . . 
and if so, the evaluation would likely 
be followed by such action as increased 
fees, extended promotion, improving 
staff supervision and conditions . . . 
One might say that to evaluate in¬ 
volves finding out what happens 
throughout the operation with a view 
to taking action for improvement. 

“Finding out what happens”, how¬ 
ever, may be a complicated assignment, 
particularly in the realms of program 
and personnel. It is not what someone 
thinks happens, or what some else 
hopes happens, but what actually does 
happen, that we’re after. 

When we have this accurate, factual 
information, we evaluate by relating 
this story of what happens, to those 
things we held as objectives; which pre¬ 
supposes that objectives are clearly 
written or thought out. 

To evaluate then, we must: 


(a) develop means of securing factual 
information. 

(b) clarify our objectives. 

(c) relate the information to the ob¬ 
jectives with a view to appraising 
the operation and . . . 

(d) take action for improvement 
where indicated. 

All four steps comprise a process and 
it is recognized that the process is most 
effective when the persons affected 
have a share in it. 

In camping, with our growing, deve¬ 
loping standards and ideals, it is surely 
most important to keep our objectives 
and standards abreast of the times. 
Hence the great importance of a Gamp 
Director’s familiarity with the latest 
and most advanced thinking regarding 

Personnel 

Program 

Staff Training 

Health and Sanitation 

Safety 

Administrative Procedures 
Buildings and equipment 

. . . for without the stimulation that 
such thinking brings, his will not likely 
be the enlightened leadership that a 
sound evaluation process needs and 
deserves. 

Our greatest weakness it seems, is in 
so frequently assuming that we evalu¬ 
ated our operation when it is the very 
deliberateness, the planned involvement 
of people, and the striving for genuine 
objectivity that differentiates the pro¬ 
cess of evaluation from that of 4 ‘sum¬ 
ming up”. 

Many aids and checklists are avail¬ 
able to us Gamp Directors, and a few 

turn to page 26 


14 


Canadian Camping 


Many campers who enjoy the woods 
and out-of-doors during the warmer 
seasons, may not have discovered that 
their favourite trails can be equally 
enjoyable when travelled on skis. 

Those who have not kindled a fire on 
the snow and eaten lunch in the open 
during the winter, may imagine that it 
would prove difficult and uncomfort¬ 
able. Having enjoyed this experience 
some hundreds of times, along Lauren- 
tian Ski Trails, during the past twenty- 
five winters, I can assure anyone who is 
interested that it is both easy and most 
enjoyable. 

These suggestions may prove helpful 
for anyone not experienced in winter 
camping: 

1. The choice of a desirable site 
for lunch is important. A sheltered 
sunny location with sufficient dry wood 
handy is ideal. 

2. Having chosen the site, gather 
all the wood that will be required, be¬ 
fore removing skis. Use only dry wood, 
maple is best, but other types may be 
used if necessary. Look for small dead 
trees or dead branches on large trees. 
No axe is necessary, as small dead 
sticks can be broken easily. As the 
wood is gathered stand it on end in the 
snow near where the fire is to be be 
built. This, of course, is to keep the 
wood free from snow. 

3. Now remove skis and kick some 
snew away from the spot where the 
fire is to be built, then tramp down the 
remainder. Powder snow will not pack 
but it will be considerably settled and 
that is all that is necessary. After the 
fire has been burning for a few minutes, 
the snow around the fire will pack hard 
under foot, so one will be standing on 
a packed surface, rather than in loose 
snow. 

4. Next, break some of the larger 
sticks into approximately two-foot 
lengths and lay several layers of these 
on the snow to form a base for the 
fire. These base logs will keep the 
snow from melting away quickly, 


COOKINC 
ON THE 
TRAIL 

by F. M. Van Wagner, 

Director, Camp Nominingue 
Faculty Adviser, McGill Outing Club . 

forming a hole under the fire resulting 
in fire going out. These foundation 
logs burn slowly, but will last as long 
as required. 

5. To start the fire use paper, 
birch bark, or small dead twigs from 
base of evergreens. Standing dead 
wood is usually drier in winter than 
summer and burns very readily. Before 
starting fire, see that there is sufficient 
wood broken into convenient lengths 
handy. 

6. A green stick can now be in¬ 
serted in the snow on which to hang 
the tea pail. Start by packing the pail 
full of snow. As the snow melts add 
chunks of snow rather than trying to 
put powder snow into pail, as that 
usually results in some snow falling into 
the fire. 

7. At most it will require about 
five minutes longer than in summer to 
make tea under these conditions. 
Therefore lunch can easily be pre¬ 
pared and eaten within an hour. 

8. There should be a fire for each 
four to six skiers so each one may 
have a place near the fire at all times, 
where he may share its warmth and 
prepare his lunch. To keep warm on 
a cold day, one must remain close to 
the fire. 

9. For a quick lunch, sandwiches 
are ideal. They may be toasted on a 

turn to page 26

NEWS AND NOTES 

FROM THE PROVINCES 


ALBERTA: 

Jim Norquay writes that the Alberta 
Camping Association held a “Leader¬ 
ship Course for Camp Counsellors” at 
Red Deer May 6th - 8th. The Con¬ 
ference was well attended and partici¬ 
pation was enthusiastic. However, some 
of the Counselors found that the pro¬ 
gramme was too advanced for them. 

Consideration is being given to hold¬ 
ing next year’s course at a camp site 
with financial help from government 
sources. 


MANITOBA: 

Mrs. J. H. McDonald was honoured 
with a Life Membership in the Mani¬ 
toba Camping Association at their 
Camping Clinic on April 9th, 1960. In 
making this presentation to Mrs. 
Armytage, Mrs. McDonald’s daughter, 
Mrs. Rook made the following state¬ 
ment: 

“It is an honour for me this evening 
to present a life membership in the 
Manitoba Camping Association to Mrs. 
J. H. McDonald. 

“Mrs. McDonald has been interested 
in our Association for many years and 
winterize a number of our existing 


on numerous occasions has helped us 
by her enthusiasm and staunch sup¬ 
port. She has been a vice-president of 
the Canadian Camping Association, 
thereby providing a valued link with 
the West, and during quite a long 
period she was able to attend the meet¬ 
ings of the Canadian Camping Associ- 
tion in Toronto. 

“Mrs. McDonald was largely res¬ 
ponsible for securing a new campsite 
for the Winnipeg Area Girl Guides, 
and as Camp Committee Chairman 
she was entirely responsible for all the 
work done in establishing the wonder¬ 
ful camp they now enjoy. 

“The doctor would not permit her 
to be with us this evening due to her 
recent illness. We regret that we are 
unable to present this certificate to her 
in person, but she has delegated her 
daughter, Mrs. J. W. G. Armytage, to 
accept it for her. We know how inter¬ 
ested Mrs. McDonald has always been 
in camping and what it offers to young 
people. She told me recently how valu¬ 
able she believed it to be and is proud 
that her own children and grand child¬ 
ren are good campers. 

“We salute a lady who is progressive 
in outlook and young in heart!”

Canadian Campino 






WHY NOT WINTERIZE 


YOUR GAMP? 

Barry G. Lowes 

Director s Camp Timberlane 


Summer is the least beautiful of the 
four seasons. How many times have 
you been at camp in the fall when the 
trees were ablaze with colour, or in the 
winter when the sun sparkled daz- 
zlinglv from the frozen lake, or thrilled 
to the warming spring thaw, and 
wished that your campers could be 
there to share it with you? It is really 
a shame that the indescribable beauty, 
the different activities possible and the 
special intimacy and adventure of 
other-season camping are not available 
to our campers. 

At Timberlane, we are beginning to 
cabins and designing new buildings for 
multiple use so that we may begin to 
enjoy winter camping. 

This article will not deal with the 
varied and unique programme possibi¬ 
lities inherent in winter camping; an¬ 
other article could follow on this 
subject. 

This article will only suggest a few 
simple, inexpensive ways of winterizing 
your buildings. Architects may suggest 
better, more expensive methods. How¬ 
ever. there are thousands of families 
living in Canada’s north country today 
in temperatures that drop far below 
zero in homes that are winterized in the 
ways described herein. First, let’s look 
at some problems to be solved. 


The most important fact to remem¬ 
ber is that cold seems to come up 
through the floor while heat escapes 
through the roof. These two areas must 
be attacked first. Then again, large 
areas of glass radiate a tremendous 
amount of heat. Doors and cracks also 
bleed a considerable heat from any 
building. 

A building that is high off the 
ground is very difficult to winterize 
because of the cold winds that whistle 
under it. To winterize any cabin effec¬ 
tively, you must close off the cabin 
underneath to block off the circulation 
of cold air. Consequently, you should 
select cabins to be winterized that are 
already sitting low to the ground. It 
is then a simple matter to seal off the 
underside of the building. 

The best and the permanent method 
is to dig a foundation, then build a 
cement block or stone foundation up 
to the floor level. However, this is 
expensive and not necessary in many 
instances. 

There are several simpler and cheaper 
methods of accomplishing this. Com¬ 
mon sheeting or any scrap lumber is 
nailed around the base of the building. 
Then earth is banked against these 
boards to completely seal off the found¬ 
ation. 


Toronto, Canada, December, 1960 


17 






Another method is to build a second 
row of boards about 12" out beyond 
the first row. Into this trough, shavings 
arc heaped in place of earth. Logs can 
be banked against the building in place 
of lumber and then heaped over with 
earth to seal the cracks. 

FLOOR. There is one more thing 
that you must do to keep the cold from 
penetrating the floor. You will need a 
double floor. 

Over your existing floor, staple or 
tack a covering of vapour barrier 
paper. Then lay your second floor 
over it. This is sufficient to keep out 
cold and dampness from below. Some 
people carry this step much further 
and are able to avoid sealing off the 
foundation. Then use aluminum foil 
rockwool insulation, and impregnated 
ten-test under the joists to provided an 
insulated floor that gives good pro¬ 
tection from winter winds. 

WALLS. In your cabins the 2x4 
studding is probably showing. These 
studs must be covered with a second or 
inside wall with the insulating material 
between the inside and outside walls. 

Rolls of fibre glass insulation that 
are paper covered and fit perfectly be¬ 
tween 22 inch centered studs can be 
bought fairly cheaply at any building 
supply company. They have ready¬ 
made tabs that facilitate stapling them 
to the studs. 

You will notice that I keep referring 
to stapling rather than nailing. For 
less than five dollars you can buy a 
small gun type stapler that will save 


you many man hours on your screen¬ 
ing, insulating, craft and multitudinous 
other camp jobs. 

These logs, boards and earth MUST 
be removed in the spring in order to 
allow the free circulation of air under 
the cabin to prevent dry rot. Some 
people run two lengths of old stove¬ 
pipe through the earthen wall, one on 
each side of the building. This permits 
enough air to circulate to prevent 
dampness from invading the founda¬ 
tion of the cabin during the winter. 

Once the fibre glass has been fasten¬ 
ed between the studs, the inside wall 
is nailed on. I have found that 3/16" 
plywood, underlay grade is the least 
expensive plywood yet it gives you a 
draft free, tightly sealed wall that goes 
on fast. 

Another method of insulating walls 
is to use dry, loosely packed shavings 
between the walls. These shaving come 
baled and cost next to nothing. The 
easiest way to use them is with tongue 
and groove boards forming your in¬ 
side wall. You begin by nailing these 
boards on the studding up to a height 
of about three feet. Then shovel the 
shavings down behind these boards 
until the space is full. Then you con¬ 
tinue to build the boards higher and 
higher, filling in behind as you go with 
shavings until the walls have all been 
insulated. The boards do not make as 
neat a job as plywood. However, they 
are much easier to work with. 

This same principle can be applied 
using shavings and plywood. Plywood 
is tricky to work with since you must 
nail it two-thirds of the way up, then 


18 


Canadian Camping 


jam a block of wood in each side to 
hold it open at the top while you shovel 
in the shavings. We use plywood and 
find that the neater finish justifies the 
extra work involved. 

If a layer of vapour barrier paper is 
put behind the plywood, any possibility 
of dampness is eliminated. This is one 
of those optional extras that is well 
worth the small expenditure of time 
and money. 

Ten-test wall board nailed over the 
studding makes an inside wall that has 
surprising insulating qualities. It does 
not require fibre glass or wood shavings 
as added insulation between the walls. 
The only drawback to ten-test is its 
fragility. It is really a pressed fibre 
type of board which is easily broken 
by a heavy blow. Cabins that will 
receive heavy boisterous summer use by 
campers should probably not be lined 
with ten-test. If the cabin will be used 
with normal care, then ten-test is a 
fine insulating wall board. Remember 
though that adding insulation between 
the walls will still add greatly to the 
cabin’s warmth. 


WINDOWS. Our windows are 
either fixed glass or screened, with 
drop-shutters. The glass is installed by 
using 2x4 blocking with pine lattice 
strips nailed around the glass both in¬ 
side and out. It is fast and also easy 
to repair should a window be broken. 
To winterize we add a second pane of 
glass inside the first using a narrower 
half-inch strip of pine lattice to hold it 
in place. Thus a double window is 
formed that works efficiently. 

Toronto, Canada , December, 1960 


Our screened, summer openings are 
covered over with a heavy tar paper. 
Then the shutters are fastened down 
tightly. The heat leakage from these 
seems to be minimal. 

ROOF. You have probably noticed 
that it is always at least twenty degrees 
warmer just under the roof of a build¬ 
ing in either summer or winter. Since 
heat rises, the heat loss through the 
roof is greater than anywhere else. To 
heat any building properly, you must 
have a ceiling. 

Ten-test wall board makes a fine, 
inexpensive ceiling or plywood may be 
used. Ten-test may be used alone with¬ 
out adding any insulation above it, 
while plywood is not as successful. For 
the best job, either fibre glass batts, 
loose insulation, or loose shavings 
should be set in above the ceiling. Now 
you almost have a snug building. 

ICING. If your cabin has boxed-in 
eaves, cut the eave off from the insu¬ 
lated area when you line your ceiling. 
The best protection against ice piling 
up on the edge of your roof and then 
backing up under the shingles is to be 
sure of a very steep pitch to the roof or 
that the roof extension is not subject 
to great changes of temperature. 


DOOR. Drafts under a door can 
steal much heat. Put weather stripping 
around it to ensure a tight seal. If 
you want added protection, build a 
small, enclosed entrance or lean-to oh 
the outside of the door. This is merely 

19 



a small sloping roof and two side walls 
that will keep the drifting snow and 
chilling winds from your door. It is 
also a good place to keep a broom for 
brushing off excess snow before enter¬ 
ing the cabin. 

All you need now is a source of heat. 


HEATING. A good box stove that 
takes 18" logs will throw off a terrific 
heat and almost roast you. Of course, 
it needs attending regularly and a good 
dry supply of wood must be laid in 
each fall. If you have plenty of wood 
available, then this is the most econ¬ 
omical method of heating. 


FIRE SAFETY. Be sure that you set 
the stove up off the floor. A frame two 
inches high with a sheet metal covering 
makes the best base. The stove pipes 
must be in good condition (cleaned 
annually) and must not run close to 
a wall or the ceiling. Unless the wall 
or ceiling is lined with gyproc or asbes¬ 
tos wall board in the vicinity of these 
stove pipes, you risk a fire. The stove 
pipe leading out of a cabin can often 
run through a window and thus save 
cutting a hole in the wall. Replace the 
glass with a piece of gyproc cut to 
size. The stove pipe outside the cabin 
should run up above roof. 


DANGER: Keep all kerosene, Naptha 
and other liquid fuels away from wood 
stoves. 

A safer, more uniform but more ex¬ 
pensive method of heating is with oil. 
Oil space heaters, (there are sizes for 
every need), are easily installed, need 
no attention, and the cabin will remain 
at a uniform temperature. Mount two 
connected oil drums on a stand out¬ 
side the cabin, higher than the stove 


intake valve. A copper tube will feed 
the oil to the stove automatically by 
gravity. 

DANGER: Should the flame in the 
stove go out, do not try to re-light the 
stove until it has cooled down enough 
to allow you to place your hand on top 
of it. If you try to light a hot stove, it 
will probably explode. 

Propane gas heaters are also avail¬ 
able. All other heating precautions 
apply to this type of heater plus the 
danger of explosions and asphyxiation 
from leaks. 

If you use these simple winterizing 
methods, you will have cabins that 
will be warm in the winter and cool 
in the summer. Winterize one cabin 
to be used solely for sleeping, another 
as a kitchen-dining room, and a third 
as a recreation cabin. 

Another time we might talk about 
plumbing, toilets, sewage, etc. It can 
be costly and difficult. However, if 
you keep your groups small, the simple 
pioneer methods can be used. 

Water is no problem. The lake is 
full of it and there is something magi¬ 
cal about chopping through the ice in 
the morning to draw a couple of pails 
of water. Take time to pause, look out 
over the lake, listen to the silence, 
drink in the stillness, the serenity and 
the peace that only the north can give. 

Share this magic with your campers. 
Plan to winterize some of your build¬ 
ings this year.

rather well . . .

to maintain their high teaching stand¬ 
ards unless assisting staff are punctual 
at all times.

time is a little short, to confine our 
attentions to one or two important 
things which have come up.

difficult for any group of women to live 
happily together for eight weeks unless 
we all make an effort to co-operate in 
every way.

your summer with us, I am sure. Per¬ 
haps another year you might find it 
challenging to try a (a) larger, (b) 
smaller, (c) different, (d) American 
camp.

Canadian Camping 




MUFFET 


by Catherine Van Wagner 
Camp Nominingue. 


Campers found Muffet one after¬ 
noon behind their tent—a furry, black 
and white shivering mite, wet from an 
all night rain. In a cage from the 
Nature Cabin they carried him up to 
our cottage. Frightened by the jostling 
and excited chattering, he stood de¬ 
fiantly in one corner—stiff-legged with 
tail curved over his back. In the warm 
kitchen, when all was quiet, he relaxed 
and began to move about. Bread and 
milk in the cage did not interest him. I 
put on gloves as a precaution and took 
him by the back of his neck into my lap. 
He snuggled down under my hand and 
went to sleep. So our “wild” baby 
skunk was tamed! One of my fondest 
dreams was realized and then and 
there I lost my heart! But more prac¬ 
tical thoughts first — how to feed him? 
Failing in all attempts with bread and 
milk and shredded meat, a doll’s plastic 
feeding bottle was produced. After a 
few squirts, he began to swallow the 
warm milk and soon, warm and full, 
was curled up on a piece of flannel 
in (yes, you guessed it) a muffet box! 
This, inside a larger carton was his 
home for a few days. Soon he was 
taking two ounces four times a day. 
Two a.m. feedings were necessary the 
first three nights. He was cold and 



lonely, and cried pitifully, but cuddled 
in a warm lap when picked up — 
just like a kitten or puppy. At meal 
times he snatched at the bottle and 
clung with his paws till the last drop 
went down. This was a favourite shot 
for camp photographers. Held by the 
back of his neck, a daily dip in a 
coffee tin was a must for cleanliness. 
He shut his eyes tightly, with never a 
struggle. We read all the articles avail¬ 
able on skunks, and decided he must 
be about five weeks old, that being 
the age when Mother Skunk thinks 
her family is able to go with her for 
an evening stroll. As the litter aver¬ 
ages five in number, and they trail 
behind her single file, it is easy to 
understand how one could get lost. We 
did wonder why his mother did not 
hear his wails when he lost touch with 
the procession, but likely she was dis¬ 
tracted by complaints from all the 
others and did not count noses on 
arrival at the burrow! 

Certainly baby skunks have voices, 
and use them. Their eyesight must not 
be very keen, for he would settle back, 
raise his sharp little black nose and 
squeal loudly when the feet he was 
following got more than three feet 
ahead. When he caught up he clung 
tightly to one’s ankle. He especially 
liked woolly socks and slacks and had 
a nap if anyone stood or sat still long 
enough. If the walk was too far, he 


Toronto, Canada, December , 1960 


23 


complained continually and had to be 
carried home — being cuddled and 
having his neck scratched was his great 
pleasure and sometimes he made con¬ 
tented low chirpy sounds. We spoiled 
him terribly. 

After the first day, a few visitors at 
a time were allowed and campers came 
in droves to admire, touch and play 
in the grass with Muffet when he was 
awake. He slept a lot and in the midst 
of playing would tuck his head far be¬ 
tween his front legs and stay in a 
rounded hump, even when put back in 
his box. When awake, Muffet followed 
closely anyone’s feet and was both a 
nuisance and a menace, but so amus¬ 
ing and irresistible that we cheerfully 
stepped over and around him — that 
is , except once when the Chief stepped 
on his tail in the living room. There 
was a decided skunky odor for some 
time, but no spray! The scent glands 
contain the secretion at birth, but the 
shooting action does not occur until 
around 9 or 10 weeks, so we felt fairly 
safe. 

After a week, Muffet spent mornings 
in a roomy pen beside the Nature 
Cabin and made many friends. He was 
always ready for play and, missing his 
own family, he chewed and tussled with 
campers’ feet and hands, or a stick, till 
he fell asleep in someone’s lap. 

Too restless now at night for a house 
pet, Muffet lived in his camp pen with 
a box for shelter and some shade pro¬ 
vided. and the wire sunk into the 
ground. Skunks are diggers and he 
evidently spent some of the night mak¬ 
ing holes, whether looking instinctively 
for grubs and beetles, or trying to 
escape — who knows? At 7 weeks he 
began to eat meat, eggs and table 
scraps, with always the same behav¬ 
iour at meals. He jumped into the 
plate and pounded the food with front 
feet! No doubt in the wild he would 


have to pounce on his dinner and hold 
it down. 

He was happy and frisky when taken 
out of the pen for a walk. One day he 
followed a camper on to the beach 
and without hesitation, into the water 
and soon was actually swimming. We 
were certainly learning about skunks! 
When playing he often pranced back 
and forth with stiff legs and tail held 
high as possible. This posture, to 
people with reservations about skunks 
large or small was a bit alarming. At 
about 9 weeks we began to notice a 
strong aroma at times and it was de¬ 
cided with reluctance to have Muffet 
made safe for camp life. There was 
always the chance that a visitor with 
a dog might be the first victim. 

Sad to relate, the poor little fellow 
did not survive the anaesthetic and 
the whole camp felt the loss of a lively, 
bright little pet. 

Our experience points to the de¬ 
sirability of having the operation per¬ 
formed at an earlier age — not more 
than 4 to 5 weeks, if a baby skunk is 
to be a really safe pet for the whole 
summer. If a family pet, a skunk is 
fairly reliable, but camp life is apt to 
prove too exciting. 

There is the thought that he would 
be defenceless if he turned back to the 
wild state, but there will always be 
someone wanting to take him home, 
in our case at least 100 campers! 

Next summer a late evening pro¬ 
gram is to be organized. A mother 
skunk with family in tow will be fol¬ 
lowed at a discreet distance and the 
baby last in line will be snatched when 
he lags behind. Scoffers say this plan 
is about on par with salting a bird’s 
tail, but we have high hopes that it 
will produce Muffet II.

forked stick to provide a warm lunch, 
which is highly recommended in cold 
weather. Frankfurters, sausages, bacon

10. If squatting or sitting on heels 
near fire is not comfortable, evergreen 
boughs laid on the snow or skis with 
running surface down will make a 
satisfactory seat 

11. Plan in advance each step to be 
taken, choose your site only after you 
have located the dead wood for the 
fire. Have each member of the party 
help with preparations and you will 
find after very little experience, that 
the lunch hour is one of the pleasant¬

12. Finally, carry an extra sweater 
and put it on as soon as you stop. Stop 
for lunch as soon as the first member 
of the party feels hungry.

CAMPING 



Winter camping can be fun. It pre¬ 
sents a few problems not met in sum¬ 
mer camping, but none that careful 
planning cannot solve. The enthusiastic 
camper will accept such problems as a 
challenge. Learning to cope with them 
brings its own reward in a sense of 
accomplishment. 

The present interest in winter camp¬ 
ing probably derives its impetus from 
experience gained by ski troops during 
the late war. When it was discovered 
that with proper equipment, living out 
of doors in winter was not too difficult, 
it was only natural that out-door 
minded people should turn to it as a 
new and interesting experience. Boy 
Scouts, and college outing clubs in 
particular, have taken the lead in this 
relatively new field of camping. It 
should not be long before our summer 
camps discover ways of promoting at 
least a limited amount of winter camp¬ 
ing. 

The McGill University Outing Club 
has been lunching around open fires 
on their weekly ski tours for the past 
15 years. Having found this to be a 


WINTER 


F . M. Van Wagner, 

Director: Camp Nominingue 
Faculty Adviser: McGill Outing Club. 


very simple and pleasant experience on 
almost any winter day in the Lauren- 
tians it was a natural step to sleeping 
out. The first experience proved so 
successful that it has now become quite 
common for small groups of outing 
club men and women to spend the 
night with sleeping bags in the snow, 
rather than occupy a bed in the M.O.- 
C. house. 

To introduce inexperienced mem¬ 
bers to the art of winter camping, the 
M.O.C. (McGill Outing Club) con¬ 
ducts three or four one night “camp- 
outs” during the winter. There may be 
from four to sixteen men and women 
on these outings. A brief description of 
the methods used by the M.O.C. 
follows. 

Previous camping experience is not 
required; anyone who can secure a 
suitable sleeping bag may join the 
party. It has been found most desirable 
to work in small groups of 4 to 5 with 
an experienced leader in charge. There 
may be from one to four such groups, 
each completely self-sufficient, camping 
in close proximity. 

These outings are usually for one 
night with 3 or 4 meals eaten out 


Toronto, Canada , December 9 1960 


27 



Clear fairly cold moonlight nights are 
preferred. Temperatures from zero to 
20 degrees above are ideal. Below zero 
temperatures present no great piob- 
leins, but of course, require warm 
sleeping bags. No tent is used, but 
each party builds a large bough lean-to 
for protection against wind or snow. 
Thick bough beds are built on the 
snow. 

A camp site is chosen that gives good 
protection from any wind, and where 
boughs and fire wood are available. A 
good wood supply is very important. 
For a lasting fire maple is best, but if 
not available, other hard woods may be 
used. Small standing dead trees, or the 
dead branches at the base of evergreens 
will provide all the dry wood required. 
When making camp, and before re¬ 
moving skis, a good supply of wood is 
gathered. 

Building a fire on the snow presents 
one problem, that of the snow melting 
beneath the fire, leaving a deep hole 
into which the fire tends to fall. This 
problem is easily solved by building 
the fire on a good foundation of green 
logs. If possible, cut a half dozen or 
so green hardwood logs 4" to 6" in 
diameter and 2 feet in length. Select 
the site for your fire, and tramp the 
snow down, then lay the green log base 
on which the fire is to be built. If 
unable to secure large green logs, 
several layers of smaller sticks will 
serve the purpose faily well. The snow 
will eventually melt around the fire as 
well as below it after the fire has been 
burning a few hours. Even in snow 3 
or 4 feet deep, a large hole will be 
melted clear to the ground. This melt¬ 
ing area may eventually be large 
enough to accommodate the whole 
party. 

To remain warm and comfortable in 
cold weather, one must either keep 
moving or stay close to the fire. A 


rather small hardwood fire gives a good 
steady heat and will keep one warm 
who squats or sits close to it. Not very 
heavy clothing is required to keep 
warm when travelling or when setting 
up camp. For most people the follow¬ 
ing is about the right amount of cloth¬ 
ing to wear at one time: medium 
weight, long wool underwear, wool ski 
slacks with smooth finish that will not 
hold the snow, a flannel shirt, a med¬ 
ium weight wool sweater, a wind 
breaker, one pair of light and one pair 
of heavy wool socks, inner wool and 
outer leather mitts, and a ski cap. In 
addition, the following extra articles of 
clothing should be carried: one or two 
pairs of socks, inner wool mitts, and 
one additional sweater or shirt. 

One of the most important consider¬ 
ations when camping out in cold 
weather is to keep dry. This usually 
means avoiding perspiration at all 
costs. In warm weather we are accus¬ 
tomed to accept perspiration as a 
natural thing when exercising. When 
travelling on skis even in the coldest 
weather, great care must be exercised 
to avoid perspiring. At the first indi¬ 
cation of being too warm, one should 
stop and remove a sweater, wind- 
breaker or shirt if necessary. This 
clothing should be put on again as soon 
as one stops. At the end of the day, 
socks should be changed. Damp socks 
should be dried before the fire with 
cither the feet or hands in them to 
avoid burning. Never, of course, try 
to warm feet near the fire with boots 
on for, as every camper should know, 
too much heat is ruinous to leather. 

No fires are kept burning at night, 
so the sleeping bags must be warm. 
There is a difference of opinion about 
what clothing should be worn in the 
sleeping bag, but whatever one wears 
must be dry. Any damp clothing 
should, if possible, be dried before the 
fire and taken in the sleeping bag, so 


28 


Canadian Camping 



it will be warm and dry the next morn¬ 
ing. Ski boots should also be put in¬ 
side the sleeping bag or they will 
freeze and be hard to get on in the 
morning. 

Two light down-filled sleeping bags 
are better than one heavy bag. Those 
used by the U.S.A. Ski Troops are 
ideal if obtainable. They consist of a 
close fitting inner (mummy) bag and 
a slightly larger outer bag, both with 
zippers. The pair weigh about 10 lbs., 
and are adequate in temperatures of 
20 degrees below zero. When sleeping 
out in cold weather, something extra 
is required underneath the body. 
Boughs help but extra clothing, card¬ 
board carton, or newspaper are good. 

Of course, eating out of doors in 
winter presents some problems not en¬ 
countered in warm weather, but any¬ 
one with a little camping experience 
can quickly learn to cope with them. 
For these short camping periods snow 
is used for water, so it is not necessary 
to camp near a lake or stream. 

When the evening meal is finished, 
the entire party gathers around one 
large fire for an enjoyable hour or two 
before retiring. Here is one occasion 
where a planned program is un¬ 
necessary. The novelty of the situation 
provides a natural topic for conversa¬ 
tion, and story telling or group singing 
follow quite naturally until the call 
of the cosy sleeping bag becomes 
irresistible. 

An evening spent around a blazing 
log fire, enjoying its warmth, on a 
bright moonlight winter night will 
match one’s most enjoyable experiences 
in the out-of-doors, and will certainly 
provide lasting memories. Yes, winter 
camping is fun. 

—• 


Toronto , Canada, December , 1960 


WOOD FIRE AND 
CANDLELIGHT 

by Mary 5 . Edgar 

A CAMP RECIPE 

A lake-bowl of water, hill-rimmed 
and blue 

Sprinkle with sunshine, diffused 
through and through 
Flavouring from miles of evergreen 
trees 

Stir altogether with clear northern 
breeze. 

Add a flash of white wings, the dash 
of a brook 

Or a slow-dropping stream from a 
fern-hidden nook. 

Allure all the children from all kith 
and kin. 

And after much sorting, and much 
merry din 

Place them in cabins where each has 
a friend. 

Provide them with fun and some 
leisure to spend. 

Season with crafts, with sailing and 
trips, 

With riding and tennis, canoeing 
and dips. 

Toast by a fire, or bake in the sun 
Until every camper is perfectly done. 
Keep them in safety eight weeks, or 
till brown: 

Then they are ready to serve back 
in town. 

I HAVE A MOUNTAIN 
I have a mountain in my soul 
For pilgrimage and far-off goal 
No landscape is completely fair 
Unless in dream’s my mountain’s there. 
I see it wrapped in mists of dawn 
Rose tinted, shy, a thing withdrawn, 
Shadow and sun it wears at noon, 

At dusk it clasps a crescent moon. 
Since first I loved a high blue hill 
Long, low horizons never fill 
The need I have for peaks that rise 
To catch the light of changing skies.

Sermons 

Winhtt 

c §s>un 



The Sunday service at camp need 
not always centre its climax in a short 
talk by the director or Senior Staff 
member. It can easily and effectively 
take the form of a service of sheer 
praise and thanksgiving. A Natur¬ 
alist’s Prayer, submitted by Mr. David 
C. Maddox, of Woodland Gamp, 
Ottawa, lends itself in an ideal way to 
worship “which finds God in the beauty 
of nature”, and which can be adapted 
to include participation by the entire 
camp group, with the director or visit¬ 
ing clergyman taking the lead. 

Should you wish to use Mr. Maddox’ 
Naturalist’s Prayer alone, simply omit 
the Call to Worship, the suggested 
hymns and the Psalm readings follow¬ 
ing the first Hymn, and headed 
“Leader”. 

Call To Worship: “Worship the Lord 

in the beauty of holiness, let all the 


earth worship his Holy Name.” 

(Chanted by selected campers from 
the rear of the group). 

Leader: We thank Thee, Oh Lord, 
for the jewelled beauty of this thy 
wonderful world. For the great 
green emerald of grass and tree, of 
shrub and flower. For thy ruby of 
the setting sun set in the gold of 
evening sky. For the topaz of the 
rising moon and the flashing dia¬ 
mond of the noon-day sun set in the 
greatest sapphire of them all, the 
blue sky. 

We thank Thee for the wonder and 
delight of rock and mineral, of 
flower and fossil, of bird and insect 
and all the infinite variety of thy 
nature. 

Let us see in it all Thine own beauty.

“TAYLOR STATTEN” 


A Biography by C. A. M. Edwards . 

REVIEWED BY MARY S. EDGAR 


This is a book which needed to be 
written. It is true that there is a great 
company of Canadians in every area 
of our wide land who could never 
forget Taylor Statten. We of the Can¬ 
adian Camping Association are among 
that vast number. He will always live 
for us as a warm and vivid personality 
who gave himself whole-heartedly to 
every forward step in establishing the 
camping movement in our land. But 
there will grow up generations ot 
campers, counsellors and directors and 
youth workers who should also know 
Taylor Statten. For them this book 
must serve as an introduction to a 
great man who was for so many of us a 
personal friend. 

I am glad that the author began at 
the beginning of “the long trail” and 
led us back to Taylor’s boyhood in the 
little village on the banks of the Credit 
River. To many of us the discovery 
that the famous showman P. T. Bar- 
num was a distant cousin and a hero 
of the growing boy, explains in part, 
the gaiety and mischief with which he 
often enlivened a rather dull meeting. 
He always took his work seriously, 
whatever new project he envisioned, 
but he never took himself too seriously 
to indulge in a good-natured joke. 

In the early days of the Canadian 
Camping Association we were a small 
and diversified group of Camp Direc¬ 
tors representing widely different types 
of camps. Some of us were groping 
beginners and some a bit cock-sure 


about our own ideas but Taylor, our 
first President, could always see the 
other person’s point of view and find 
value in it. His leadership in welding 
us into a truly cooperative group can¬ 
not be measured. It was a very proud 
moment for many of us when we 
watched him take his place in Washing¬ 
ton D.C. as President of the American 
Camping Association — the first and 
only Canadian to be elected to that 
office. 

Perhaps the privilege of reviewing 
this book was given to me because 
“the long trail” takes me back to the 
days when Taylor Statten was making 
a great name for himself in boys’ work. 
It was at Camp Couchiching in 1910 
that I first became acquainted with 
Mr. and Mrs. Statten and their small 
curly haired daughter, Adele. Per¬ 
haps the author does not realize that 
the Y.W.C.A, and Girls’ Work in Can¬ 
ada also owe a great debt to him. 
When the first committee work was 
done on the Canadian Girls in Train¬ 
ing program, we were greatly indebted 
to him for the ideas he had already 
worked out for boys. 

It was his great ability to make 
friends which always impressed those 
of us who knew him. Quoting from 
the book: “He could discern a person’s 
problem, make it his own and suggest 
some practical solution . . . He had the 
divine quality of being able to put 
himself in the other person’s place . . . 
He was tolerant of shortcomings of

Camping has lost a staunch and 
devoted friend in John Hoyle, who 
died Oct. 18th at Haliburton, Ont. 
Born in Spain, educated in England, 
“Tlu* Major” was for many years 
active in youth and religious education 
work. For several years he was secre¬ 
tary of the Religious Education Council 
in Canada. Owner and Director of 
Camp GayVenture since its inception 
in 1946, he proved to be a vital and 
guiding influence in the lives of the 
many hundreds of boys and girls who 
passed through his hands at camp. 
Past President of the Ontario Camping 
Association, and for many years active 
on its Executive, The Major did much 
to further the high standards of camp¬ 
ing in Ontario and other parts of 
Canada. Camps and camping people 
are the poorer for his death.

others, with a sometimes disarming 
acknowledgment of his own.” These 
and many other statements in the 
biography arc facts which were fully 
demonstrated among us. 

The story of the beginnings of Camp 
Ahmek and its development through 
the years is a record every Camp 
Director will enjoy. Many will be sur¬ 
prised to learn of the diversity of 
Taylor Station's interests in art, music 
and drama, and how he so richly 
shared all these with the campers of 
Ahmek and Camp Wapomeo through 
many a happy summer. One will fol¬ 
low reverently the growth and depth of 
his religious convictions with an appre¬ 
ciation of his deep sincerity. The final 
chapter, “Algonquin Symphony'’ gives 
“The Chief’s” last letter to his campers, 
with a poignant post script added by 
“Tonekela” after he had quietly fallen 
asleep in their island cabin on his 
beloved Canoe Lake.

Leader: Give the Lord the honour due 
unto his name; Worship the Lord 
with holy worship; it is the Lord 
that commandeth the waters; it is 
the glorious God that maketh the 
thunder; it is the Lord that ruleth

At this point one of the campers 
could read a chapter or story from the 
Bible, the Beatitudes or other favourite 
reading, followed by an anthem selected 
by the choir. 

Leader: Closing prayer and blessing. 

This service would require some pre¬ 
paration, and the group readings mime¬ 
ographed or memorized beforehand. 
Favourite hymns may, of course, be 
substituted, or the director and campers 
may wish to select two or three short 
anthems to be sung by the choir. The 
Naturalist’s Prayer is adaptable in 
many ways, if the director or leader 
does wish to include a short talk as 
part of the service, or to extend the 
psalm reading beyond the limited 
space in the magazine. This would be 
an excellent opportunity to collect (or 
rent) reproductions of outdoor scenes 
and have them displayed on the lodge 
or hall walls for the occasion.

expenses have been deducted from the 
revenue there should be a credit bal¬ 
ance or profit. 

At this point consideration should 
be given to depreciation or capital cost 
allowance. The Dominion Government 
has tables showing the maximum 
amount that may be taken each year 
for depreciation and a copy of this 
portion of the Income Tax Act may be 
obtained from the Queen’s Printer in 
Ottawa so that it may be kept on file 
for future reference. It is important 
that all items — buildings, canoes, cars, 
to mention a few, be placed in their 
proper categories for depreciation over 
the years. The amount of allowance 
that you take from your gross profit is 
really a credit item as this amount 
should be set aside as a reserve for 


depreciation to purchase new equip¬ 
ment and erect new buildings when 
the existing ones are no longer useful. 

Mortgage or loan repayments could 
be the next item that must be met from 
the current year’s revenue. If making 
a loan for capital requirements make 
sure you do not agree to make prin¬ 
cipal repayments so high that it will 
take all your remaining revenue to 
meet them. Also, here we must think 
about money for new equipment or 
new buildings to either expand or im¬ 
prove your camp site and extend pro¬ 
gram possibilities. 

Income tax is an item that must be 
remembered and remitted to the pro¬ 
per place at the proper times. In a 
sole proprietorship or partnership where 
you possibly wait until the fall to see 
if you are going to make a profit, just

remember it isn’t all yours — a final 
accounting must be made with the in¬ 
come tax department. 

For a camp that has never operated 
before many of the items will be pure 
guess work and there will be many 
items of expense you never dreamed 
of. However, it is essential that you 
estimate your expected revenue and 
expenses. Above all be conservative — 
keep your expected revenue on the low 
side and make good allowances for 
your expenses — iTetter to end up with 
more profit than you expected than 
none at all. 

Consult your accountant as you 
would your doctor or lawyer, he is an 
expert in his field and can be a valu¬ 
able assistant to you in keeping your 
books straight, a credit balance instead 
of a debit and taxes all paid.

Wood Fire and Candlelight 

MY LIBRARY 

The books I love best would go on 
one shelf 

I never want cases high. 

For I have a key to a library 
With tales in the earth and sky. 

I read the lyrics of bubbling streams 
The poetry of the sea 
The fairy tal es from the glen of 
dreams 

The chronicles of the tree. 

I know the song that a vagrant wind 
To the silver birch tree sings, 

I read the scroll that the stars unroll 
And the rhymes of the humbler 
things. 

To enter this wondrous library 
You must find the magic key 
A fairy, I think in the long, long ago 
Loaned one of her keys to me.

from page 11 

painting, leathercraft, etc.). As well as 
these activities we do not overlook the 
treatments some of the children must 
continue during their stay at camp. 
Our physiotherapy hut is fully equip¬ 
ped and we employ a staff of three or 
four physiotherapists, depending upon 
their availability. I feel that a physio¬ 
therapist can accomplish much more in 
a camp than in a hospital because she 
gets to know her patients better, and 
the patients know her better, as they 
live together and both take part in 
social activities. The results of physio¬ 
therapy treatments are, therefore, more 
beneficial when carried on in a camp. 

After a year or two at our Crippled 
Children’s Camp many of the campers 
are able to attend other ordinary child¬ 
ren’s camps and become part of the 
group. In fact I encourage parents to 
send their crippled children to ordinary 
children’s camps as soon as the child 
is sufficiently prepared to make the 
changeover, but it is important for the 
parents to know the Camp Director 
where the child is to be sent. This is 
the beginning of another step forward 
in life as, in later years, the crippled 
child will be associating with normal 
people more often.

A choice of plans for all organizational, church and 
private camps providing broad medical expense 
protection for each accident and each sickness at low 
cost group rates for both campers and staff members. 

Put CAMP-GUARD on your programme. Display 
this symbol and let parents know your camp is 
covered. This symbol of outstanding coverage 
assures them you take added interest in your 
camper's welfare, by providing a CAMP-GUARD 
accident and sickness plan. 

Your local insurance agent will help you choose the 
right plan for your camp; or write our nearest office 
for full particulars.
